blocks.text: Ezra 6 records Darius's imperial investigation and decisive response to temple construction. When provincial opposition arises, Darius orders an archival search that recovers Cyrus's original authorization. Rather than suppressing the work, this discovery confirms and amplifies imperial backing through written orders, direct funding, and provisions. The chapter demonstrates how the Persian administrative system—its record-keeping, hierarchical authority, and royal decrees—became the practical means for temple restoration in the early Persian period.

Darius orders an archival search in Babylon and discovers a document at Achmetha in Media containing Cyrus's decree from his first regnal year. This narrative sequence—opposition, inquiry, archival recovery, confirmation—positions Darius not as introducing new policy but as enforcing an existing imperial authorization. Within Achaemenid provincial administration, such written records in official archives preserved distant central authority's decisions and maintained continuity of policy across the empire.

Cyrus's recorded decree specifies temple dimensions (60 cubits in both height and breadth), construction materials (stone courses and timber), and royal treasury funding. Critically, it directs restoration of the gold and silver temple vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar—aligning with Achaemenid practice of recovering cult objects as part of temple support. The recovered document thus validates the entire restoration project by anchoring it to Cyrus's original imperial authorization, establishing continuity across reigns.

Darius's direct command to Tattenai (governor beyond the River) and his colleagues marks a decisive shift from opposition to enforcement. The order—'be ye far from thence; let the work of this house of God alone'—establishes imperial will as protection for the Jewish community's project. This intervention reflects Persian provincial administration: local officials could challenge initiatives, but the king could override such opposition through hierarchical written command, using administrative structure to suppress interference.

Beyond halting opposition, Darius authorizes affirmative support through provincial taxation. Work expenses are to be drawn from 'the tribute beyond the River'—placing the temple project within the imperial fiscal system itself. This arrangement embedded the temple within provincial revenue structures, legitimizing religious institutions as appropriate beneficiaries of state resources. The practice reflects Achaemenid policy of channeling provincial tax revenue toward temples and major infrastructure projects.

The decree specifies daily provision of sacrificial animals (bullocks, rams, lambs) and staple commodities (wheat, salt, wine, oil) to Jerusalem's priests 'without fail.' These provisions align priestly instructional expertise—priests specify needed items—with imperial logistical authority. Darius's guarantee of continuous provision frames the temple not merely as a constructed facility but as a functioning institution requiring consistent resources within Persian provincial administration.

Darius frames the provision for sacrifice as enabling priestly prayers for the king's life and his sons. This reciprocity—imperial resource commitment enabling religious intercession—reflects standard Achaemenid practice. The transaction is structural rather than purely devotional: the king's authority is enhanced through religiously sanctioned support, and divine favor is invoked through properly maintained worship. The passage thus presents the temple within a broader imperial-religious economy rather than in isolation.

Darius's decree resolves the conflict: opposition dissolves through imperial inquiry and written authorization. Though explicit completion is reported later, this chapter demonstrates the administrative mechanism enabling temple restoration. The sequence—opposition, archival search, imperial confirmation, direct orders, provisional authority, and material support—illustrates how Persian administrative machinery provided the practical framework for rebuilding Jerusalem's sanctuary. Both Cyrus's original authorization (recovered in the archive) and Darius's enforcement operated through the same imperial system, culminating in the temple's completion in Darius's sixth regnal year.
